title: How to Lower Your Electric Bill Without Changing Your Life
description: How to lower your electric bill with free habits and cheap fixes: thermostat, standby power, laundry, LEDs and drafts, with a worked example.

body:
Your electric bill went up again, and you are not sure why. Nothing obvious changed. You just lived your life, and the bill still grew.

Learning how to lower your electric bill starts with one simple idea. Your bill is two numbers multiplied together: the electricity you use, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), times the price your utility charges per kWh, plus any fixed charges. Use less, and the bill falls, even if the price stays the same.

This guide walks through the fixes in order, from free habits to low-cost swaps to bigger upgrades. You do not need to buy anything to start, and nothing here asks you to sit in the dark.

## What does lowering your electric bill actually mean?

Lowering your electric bill means cutting the number of kilowatt-hours your home uses each month, or paying a lower price for each one. Most of this guide covers the first part, using less, because that is the part fully in your hands. The last section covers the second part, checking your rate plan. Both work, and they stack.

## Why is my electric bill so high?

Before you change anything, read one bill properly. Find three numbers: how many kWh you used, the price per kWh, and the fixed charges. Then compare the kWh, not just the dollars, with the same month last year. Summer and winter bills are always higher than spring and fall, so last month is a bad comparison.

For a sense of scale, the average US home used 874 kWh a month and paid $150.68 in 2025, at an average price of 17.23 cents per kWh, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA Form EIA-861, 2025 data, released October 2026). Your bill will differ by state, home size, and heating type, but that average tells you whether you are in normal territory or way above it.

The usual reasons a bill jumps: heating or cooling running longer, a new space heater, more people at home, a rate increase, or a longer billing period. If your utility has an app or online portal, check your daily usage. A sudden step up on one date usually points to one cause.

It also helps to treat electricity as a normal line in your budget, not a surprise. [How to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) shows how to give every bill a fixed place in your plan.

## What uses the most electricity in a home?

Heating and cooling are usually the biggest share of a home's electricity, which is why the thermostat is the single most powerful lever you have. After that come water heating, the fridge, and the washer and dryer. Lighting and electronics are smaller, but they add up because they run for so many hours.

One thing surprises most people: the devices that look off. TVs, game consoles, cable boxes, and chargers keep drawing a little power while plugged in. Each one is small. A whole house of them is not.

## Free habits that lower your electric bill

Start here. These cost nothing, and they work from tonight.

### 1. Turn the thermostat back when you sleep or leave

The U.S. Department of Energy estimates that turning the thermostat back 7 to 10 degrees for eight hours a day can save as much as 10% a year on heating and cooling. In winter, that means setting it lower while you sleep or while nobody is home. In summer, it means letting the house get a few degrees warmer during those same hours.

A practical starting point is 68 degrees Fahrenheit while you are awake and at home in winter, then lower at night and when you leave. If you have a heat pump, keep the change smaller. A big setback can trigger the backup heat, which wipes out the saving.

### 2. Turn things off, for real

Lights, fans, and the TV when nobody is using them. A fan cools people, not rooms, so an empty room with a running fan is pure waste. Make it a habit when you leave a room, the same way you close a door behind you.

### 3. Kill standby power

Unplug chargers when devices finish charging. Chargers keep drawing power from the outlet even when nothing is connected, according to ENERGY STAR. A power strip makes this easy: plug the TV, console, and speakers into one strip and switch it off with one flip. Do not unplug the fridge or freezer. Everything else is fair game.

### 4. Wash cold and wash full

Heating water accounts for about 90% of the energy your washing machine uses, according to ENERGY STAR. Cold water gets most everyday laundry clean, and a full load uses the same energy as a half load. Two small choices, one real saving.

### 5. Take shorter showers

Hot water costs money twice: heating it, then sending it down the drain. ENERGY STAR suggests keeping showers under five minutes. You do not need a timer. One song, then out.

### 6. Be kind to your fridge

Your fridge runs all day, every day, so small habits matter. Decide what you want before you open the door, and close it while you think. Keep the door seals clean so cold air stays inside.

### 7. Use the sun and the doors

On a sunny winter day, open the curtains on the sunny side and let the sun warm the room. On a hot summer afternoon, close them to keep the heat out. Keep doors and windows closed while the heat or air conditioning runs, and only heat or cool the rooms you actually use.

## Low-cost fixes that pay for themselves

Once the free habits are in place, these small purchases earn their cost back.

### 1. Swap your most-used bulbs to LED

ENERGY STAR certified LED bulbs use up to 90% less energy and last 15 times longer than standard bulbs. Replacing your five most frequently used light fixtures with certified bulbs can save nearly $40 a year in energy costs.

### 2. Stop the drafts

Cold air sneaking in around windows and doors makes your heater work overtime. In summer, the same gaps let cool air leak out. ENERGY STAR suggests weatherstripping drafty windows and doors. A roll of foam tape, a door sweep, or a door snake costs a few dollars and takes minutes to fit.

### 3. Change the HVAC filter

A clogged filter makes your system push harder for the same result. ENERGY STAR recommends replacing HVAC filters at least once every three months. It is a two-minute job.

### 4. Clean the dryer lint filter

Clean the lint trap before every dryer load. A clogged filter makes the dryer run longer, and longer means more electricity.

### 5. Add a smart power strip

A smart power strip cuts power to devices that sit in standby, like the TV setup, while keeping one outlet live for the device that controls it. It does the unplugging for you, every day.

## Fixes ranked by cost and effort

Use this table to pick your starting point. Free habits come first because they cost nothing and work right away.

| Fix                               | Cost               | Effort | What it saves                                                                         |
|---------------------------------------|------------------------|------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Turn the thermostat back              | Free                   | Low        | As much as 10% a year on heating and cooling (U.S. DOE)                                   |
| Turn things off, kill standby         | Free                   | Low        | Varies; standby adds up across a house                                                    |
| Wash cold, wash full, shorter showers | Free                   | Low        | Less hot water; heating water is about 90% of washer energy (ENERGY STAR)                 |
| Swap 5 most-used bulbs to LED         | A few dollars per bulb | Low        | Nearly $40 a year (ENERGY STAR)                                                          |
| Draft proofing: foam tape, door sweep | A few dollars          | Low        | Less heated or cooled air escaping                                                        |
| HVAC filter every 3 months            | A few dollars          | Low        | System runs easier (ENERGY STAR)                                                          |
| Smart power strip                     | Low                    | Low        | Standby power, automatically                                                              |
| Smart thermostat                      | Medium                 | Medium     | Setbacks happen on schedule; check for utility rebates                                    |
| ENERGY STAR appliance when replacing  | Higher                 | Medium     | A home full of ENERGY STAR products uses 24% less energy, saves about $450 (ENERGY STAR) |

## Bigger upgrades, and when they make sense

Do not replace a working appliance just to save electricity. The saving rarely covers the cost of a new machine. But when something dies, or you are buying anyway, choose an ENERGY STAR certified model. On average, a home equipped with ENERGY STAR certified products uses 24% less energy and saves about $450, according to ENERGY STAR.

A smart thermostat is the one upgrade worth considering on its own, because it automates the biggest free habit on this list. It turns the temperature back when you leave and brings it back before you return, so you do not have to remember. Many utilities offer rebates that cut the price. Check yours before you buy.

If you rent, check with your landlord before changing anything fixed, like a thermostat or windows. And if an upgrade needs saving up for, put it in a sinking fund instead of on a credit card. [Sinking funds for beginners](/blog/sinking-funds-for-beginners/) shows how to save a little each month for a planned cost like this.

## Check the price you pay, not just the power you use

Your bill has two sides: how much you use, and what you pay per kWh. Some utilities offer time-of-use plans, where electricity costs less late at night and more in the afternoon peak. If you are on one, run the dishwasher, washer, and dryer outside peak hours. If you are not sure which plan you are on, it is printed on your bill.

Ask your utility three questions: Do you offer a free energy audit? Do you have a budget billing plan that evens out seasonal spikes? Are there rebates for LEDs, thermostats, or efficient appliances?

If you share a home, agree on the split before the bill arrives, not after. [How to split bills with roommates](/blog/how-to-split-bills-with-roommates/) covers fair ways to divide utilities, including what to do when one person clearly uses more.

If the bill is genuinely hard to pay, call your utility and ask about payment plans and assistance programs. Many have them, and asking early is always better than missing a payment. Rules and programs vary by country, state, and utility, so check your own provider's terms.

## A worked example: one bill before and after

This is an illustration with made-up numbers. It shows how the math works, not what your home will save.

|               | Before | After |
|---------------|------------|-----------|
| Monthly use   | 800 kWh    | 660 kWh   |
| Price per kWh | $0.18     | $0.18    |
| Energy charge | $144.00   | $118.80  |
| Fixed charges | $12.00    | $12.00   |
| Total bill    | $156.00   | $130.80  |

The after column comes from five habit changes: thermostat setback (60 kWh less), LED bulbs and lights off (25 kWh less), cold wash and full loads (20 kWh less), standby power on strips (15 kWh less), and shorter showers (20 kWh less). That is 140 kWh less, so 800 minus 140 equals 660 kWh.

The saving is $156.00 minus $130.80, which is $25.20 a month. Over a year, that is $25.20 times 12, which is $302.40. Your numbers will differ. But the method is the same: find the kWh, cut the kWh, and the dollars follow.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why is my electric bill so high?

Usually one of three things: you used more kWh, your rate went up, or the billing period was longer. Compare the kWh on this bill with the same month last year. If the kWh jumped, look for a cause: colder or hotter weather, a space heater, guests, or an appliance struggling. If the kWh is steady but the bill rose, the rate or fixed charges changed.

### Does unplugging things really save electricity?

Yes, a little per device, and it adds up across a house. Chargers, TVs, consoles, and cable boxes draw power while plugged in, even when off. Unplugging them, or switching off a power strip, removes that draw completely.

### How can I lower my electric bill in an apartment?

Almost everything on this list works in an apartment. Thermostat habits, LEDs, power strips, cold wash, and shorter showers need no permission. Draft proofing with removable foam tape and door sweeps is renter-friendly too. For anything fixed, like a thermostat swap, ask your landlord first.

### What uses the most electricity in a home?

Heating and cooling, usually. After that, water heating, the fridge, and the washer and dryer. That is why the thermostat, hot water, and laundry habits come first in this guide. Lighting and standby power are smaller, but they are the easiest to fix.

### Does a smart thermostat actually save money?

It can, because it automates the setback habit. The thermostat turns itself back when you leave or sleep, so the saving happens even when you forget. It works best in homes where heating and cooling are a big part of the bill. Check for a utility rebate before you buy.

## Your next step

Pick two free habits from this list and start tonight. Turn the thermostat back before bed, and switch off one power strip. Then open your next bill and look at the kWh, not just the total. When you see the number drop, you will know exactly which habits did it.

If you want to track the saving, a simple budget app helps. [The best free budgeting apps](/blog/best-free-budgeting-apps/) compares free options that can hold your utility line next to the rest of your spending.

**Related:** [How to cancel subscriptions you don't use](/blog/cancel-subscriptions/), [Bill tracker](/blog/bill-tracker-template/).

This article is general information, not personal financial advice. Rates, rebates, and programs vary by country, state, and utility, so check your own provider's terms.
